E0033.summary: Cornelius Agrippa, Trithemius' pupil, author of the Occult Philosophy and the Vanity of the Sciences, cited by Atwood throughout as a witness to self-knowledge, secrecy and the inward Operator.
E0033.body:
Listed as Trithemius' pupil among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his three books of *Occult Philosophy* and his *Vanity of the Sciences* (De Vanitate Scientiarum) for the oath of secrecy and the singleness of the subject — “I could tell many tings of this art, if I had not sworn to keep silence” [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n70] — and argues that the *Vanity* is a consummation, not a recantation. From the *Vanity* she also takes the account of Alexander the Great's death by the venom of the waters of the Styx, paralleling Vaughan's [I.1 ¶74, I.1 n94]; knowledge by entering into oneself, with oblivion as impediment: “entering not either into the schools of other philosophers, but into yourself, ye shall know all things” [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n13]; and the praise of the 'asinine condition' of the disciple of Wisdom, which she applies to the Philosophic Subject: “There is no creature, concludes the panegyrist, that is so able to receive divinity as an ass” [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

From the *Occult Philosophy* (Book 3): the soul freed from the senses comprehends all; man is image of God and microcosm — “Whosoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself” [II.1 ¶9, II.1 n4]; and the pure mind laid asleep and brought into its divine nature, which Atwood endorses as alluding to Alchemy: “in us, I say, is the Operator of miracles” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n26]. She says the work expounds diffusely that imaginative impressions linger and pollute the ether of a place [III.4 ¶42].

Other uses: Scripture is no longer read “under the Bark of the Law” [III.3 ¶59]; Scripture is obscure and mystical yet significant (“Clausum est Armarium”) [IV.3 ¶46]; the two natures to be joined (“Pinge duos Angues”) [III.1 ¶50]; within Vaughan's lessons, a heavenly life as condition of communion with superiors [III.4 ¶44]; and his mature conviction that “to know Nothing was the most happy life” [IV.4 ¶27].

Atwood also qualifies him: he knew the First Preparation but not the Solution of the Salt, as his practice at Malines shows, and confessed he could not increase the transmutative virtue [IV.1 ¶36].

E0034.summary: Name a cited French source (Mystere de la Croix) gives to the work of repeated cooking until rainbow colours and heavy drops appear.
E0034.body: Quoted from the French source *Mystere de la Croix*: the work of repeated cooking, continued until the rainbow colours and heavy drops appear, is so named — “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶18]. The word renders as 'magnetic' (our translation; by: ours). The text here does not itself link it to Atwood's 'magnetic series' [III.3 ¶10].

E0035.summary: In Reuchlin, as quoted, the Hebrew name of the Absolute Essence while retracted in darkness and at rest — 'nothing as respects us'.
E0035.body: Quoted from Reuchlin: Ain names the Absolute Essence while it is retracted in darkness and at rest, and is glossed by the text itself as “Ain, i.e., to say, Nihil quoad nos; nothing or no entity as respects us” [III.2 ¶10]. It is called nothing not absolutely but relative to us, because “we, being affected with inability in the conception, do judge and imagine of those things which do not appear immediately as if they were not at all” [III.2 ¶10]. Asserted identity: Ain = Nihil quoad nos [III.2 ¶10].

E0036.summary: Figure invoked as an image of works that vanish before celestial light.
E0036.body: Invoked as an illustration: such works vanish before celestial light like “Aladdin’s rapid castle” [II.3 ¶36].

E0037.summary: Alain de l’Isle, author of the Dicta de Lapide and a commentary on Merlin's Prophecies, said to have obtained the Elixir; cited as a case of editors suppressing alchemical testimony.
E0037.body: Atwood cites him (as Alani Philosophi, Alanai de Insulis) for his *Dicta de Lapide* and his commentary on the Prophecies of Merlin (*Prophetia Anglicana Merlini*, Francf. 1608). He is said to have obtained the Elixir, and serves as an example of editors suppressing alchemical testimony [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n53, I.1 n54].

E0038.summary: Albertus Magnus, a practising alchemist by Atwood's proofs, cited for the first matter, perfect solution as the first rule, the vessel, and man as seat of the highest mineral virtue.
E0038.body:
Atwood offers proof that Albert was a practising alchemist who described the first matter and commended alchemy as the best means of inquiry, and an example of renunciation of worldly advantage; she cites *De Mineralibus*, *Libellus de Alchemia*, *Concordanditia Philosophorum de Lapide*, *Secretum Secretorum* and the *Breve Compendium*: “De transmutatione horum corporum metallicorum et mutatione unius in aliud non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶41, I.1 n45, I.1 n46]. He is named with Lully as revering Geber [I.1 ¶32].

First matter: the mercury of the wise is “a watery element, cold and moist, a permanent water” [I.2 ¶29, I.2 n27]; he agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. From the book of Minerals: the highest mineral virtue is in man — “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all, burns more than all glorious in him erect” [II.1 ¶12]; and from *De Minerabilis*, all things may be reduced to gold: “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold, is found in the ultimate alchemical analysis of every existing thing” [III.2 n38].

Solution: “The beginning of the work, says Albertus Magnus, is a perfect solution” — dissolve and recongeal, fix and volatilize [II.3 n2]; “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution”, washing the occult Arcanum ('our brass') until pure [II.2 ¶16, II.2 n15]; “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass”, purified by successive dissolution and coagulation [IV.1 ¶4, IV.1 n2].

Vessel: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]; Norton's verse says “And this sheweth best Albertus Magnus, In his Boke De Mineralibus” on the right figure of vessels [III.4 ¶31].

In quoted verse: Ripley names “Albert, Raymond and Arnolde” as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62]; Norton names “Albertus Magnus, the Black Freere” as lacking understanding of multiplying the Red Stone [I.1 ¶60].

E0039.summary: Atwood's later definition: the throwing down of the walls of the harmony-ensphered life, accompanied with noise.
E0039.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The throwing down of the Walls of this is harmony-ensphered life is the Alchemical solution” [APP ¶50]; it is accompanied with noise. Asserted identity: Alchemical solution = the throwing down of the Walls [APP ¶50].

E0040.summary: The Alchemist as agreeing with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, contrasted with modern Alchemists who are mostly silent on their Art's metaphysics.
E0040.body: Atwood says the Alchemist agrees with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, while modern Alchemists are mostly silent on the metaphysics of their Art [III.2 ¶46].

E0041.summary: The Alchemists as a collective voice Atwood draws on for the Matter, solution, the unclean Instrument, the threefold Law's periods, and the stirring of Motion.
E0041.body:
Atwood treats the Alchemists as a body of witness, generally supporting her reading:

- They recommend observing nature for analogy [I.3 n27].
- Their condemnation of the defiled vulgar Matter, and its preparation into the Mercury of the Philosophers, she links to the purification of the Spirit [II.2 ¶16]; their description of the subject — “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” — fits the Common Soul [II.2 ¶18]; their Matter is the Passive Nature: “the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].
- They supply the term dissolve for the trance change (“it ought to be dissolved”), and Black Saturn, the mineral tree, the doves [II.3 n2, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶18].
- Life is a fire imprisoned in aerial moisture (“Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi”); they warn of horrors and phantoms [II.3 ¶29].
- Their saying that there is “nothing of an unclean nature that enters into the composition of the Stone, except One thing” Atwood endorses, explaining at length that the unclean Instrument is necessary because the philosophers are obscure about it [III.1 ¶61].
- They name the three periods of the threefold Law: “called by the Alchemists, for certain accurate reason, Altitude, Latitude and Profundity” [III.3 ¶72].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): their Vulcan is decoded as Motion [APP ¶129]; and the older masters' “when Vulcan appears in the same altar with Minerva the conjunction is ominous” marks the point of passivity at which the Artist must stir up the Motion, which Atwood glosses as the stirred Wisdom-life being taken by self-will [APP ¶82].

E0042.summary: Joint witnesses asserting an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena.
E0042.body: Cited in support: the Alchemists and Greek physicians assert an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena [IV.4 ¶13].

E0043.summary: The Hermetic art: in Atwood's account an antique sacred science of vital chemistry, fermenting and purifying the human spirit by its own Light into regenerated life and relation with God.
E0043.body:
**The early account (main text).** Atwood calls it the Hermetic art, to be considered “an antique arifice coeval, for aught we know to the contrary, with the universe itself” [I.1 ¶3]; Egypt's Sacred Art, of which “This Emerald Table, unique and authentic as it may be regarded, is all that remains to us from Egypt of her Sacred Art” [I.1 ¶10], with its practical method in the *Tractatus Aureus*. She suggests it was “perhaps” stigmatized as a Black Art partly from the word Chemia [I.1 ¶5]. Now preserved in archives and despised, it is either “the acme of human folly, or contrariwise, as the recondite perfection of wisdom and causal science” [I.1 ¶76]; “the world has learned to despise alchemy, confounding the genuine doctrine with their sophistical and vile productions” [I.1 ¶53].

It concerns transmutation of metals: per Albert, “non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica”, and he “recommends alchemy as the best and most easy means of rational investigation” [I.1 ¶39]. It has nothing to do with modern chemistry: “No modern art or chemistry, notwithstanding all its surreptitious claims, has any thing in common to do with Alchemy, beyond the borrowed terms” [II.1 ¶5]; it requires the vital force, and philosophers sought it “not so much out of covetousness for gold or silver, but for the knowledge’s sake” [II.1 ¶10]. In it “the nature of things is altogether altered and ultimately reversed” and Final Causes are manifest [III.4 ¶9]. God grants it to few; its records hold the inner sense aloof from the literal, and “the Art will probably continue concealed though many ages still” [III.4 ¶16].

Norton (quoted) calls it “most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶52], holy because found only by grace: “Called this science Holy Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10]. Further verse in the same discussion affirms: “Yet is this science of Alkimy full trew;” [III.4 ¶14].

**Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).** Atwood defines it directly: “Alchemy is an universal art of vital chemistry” [APP ¶6] that ferments, purifies and dissolves the human spirit into new life; “Alchemy is a process of fermenting the vital Spirit in and by its own Light.” [APP ¶27]; “Alchemy is the art of fermenting the human vital spirit” to purify and finally dissolve it, so the principle is reconstructed through regeneration [APP ¶68]. “Alchemy goes beyond nature”, taking her up and advancing her beyond her created state [APP ¶155]. It brings man into relationship with God.

Asserted identities: = Divine Chemistry, “the transmutation of Life” [APP ¶25]; = Holy Alchemy, “called by the Adepts Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29]; = philosophy: “Alchemy is philosophy; it is the philosophy, the seeking of The Sophia in the mind.” [APP ¶183], fully understood only by those working the process.

E0044.summary: Emblem-maker whose dolphin wreathed about an anchor ('Festina Lente') Atwood applies to slow trituration.
E0044.body: Atwood applies Alciatus' emblem of a dolphin wreathed about an anchor, “Festina Lente”, to slow trituration [IV.1 ¶13].

E0045.summary: The vessel, in quoted authorities, through which the spiritualized gold passes and in which the Mercuries are cherished over fire.
E0045.body: Two quoted authorities name it. The author of *Lucerna Salis*: “by means of the spirit it passes through the Alembic, its earth remaining black” — said of the spiritualized gold [III.3 ¶32]. Flamel: “cherish them over a fire in thy Alembic”, of the Mercuries [IV.1 ¶41]. Neither passage gives a further gloss; any figurative sense would be inference.

E0046.summary: Recipient of Aristotle's avowal that only his pupils would understand the Acaomatic Ethics.
E0046.body: Named as the recipient of Aristotle's avowal that only his pupils would understand the Acaomatic Ethics [III.2 ¶40].

E0048.summary: Cited, via the Open Entrance (which a bracketed correction attributes to Philalethes), for the persecution of true adepts.
E0048.body: Cited for the *Open Entrance* (*Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palationem*, cap. xiii) to illustrate the persecution of true adepts and the danger of even healing with the medicine: “a continual banishment: deprived of the society of friends and family” [I.1 ¶66, I.1 n73]. A bracketed correction in the text attributes the work to Philalethes.

E0049.summary: Group voice cited for the teaching that initiation to the Paternal abode opens all divine paths.
E0049.body: Cited in support: initiation to the Paternal abode opens all divine paths [II.4 ¶23].

E0050.summary: The Alexandrians, cited for their enthusiasm for the Mysteries and their account of the descent and efflux of matter.
E0050.body: Their enthusiasm for the Mysteries is cited as evidence of their high regard [II.2 ¶3]. They explained the descent and efflux of matter, as if knowing the universe by analogy through their own [III.2 ¶40].

E0051.summary: 'The Arabian', cited from the Centrum Naturae Concentratum for man as producer of the true fiery water.
E0051.body: Cited from *Centrum Naturae Concentratum* in support of man producing the true fiery water: “even thou art he who through the breath and power of the water and earth in thyself, conjoinest the elements” [II.1 ¶14, II.1 n12].

E0052.summary: Radical dissolvent of the metals, per Eudoxus a true permanent water staying united with what it dissolves; elsewhere named only among alchemists' goals.
E0052.body: Named without explanation in a quoted Faraday Society address listing alchemists' goals: “the philosophers’ stone, the transmutation of metals, the alkahest, and the elixir of life” [I.1 ¶33]. Eudoxus (quoted) gives its meaning: “the great Alcahest, which radically dissolves the metals -- a true permanent water” [IV.3 ¶10], remaining inseparably united with the metals it dissolves and increasing their weight and tincture. Asserted identity: Alcahest = true permanent water [IV.3 ¶10].

E0053.summary: What, per Atwood, he possesses who knows Nothing: composed of the whole, he can discern, make and effect the whole.
E0053.body: Atwood says he who knows Nothing has the All: “being composed of the whole, he is able to discern, to make, and to effect the whole” [IV.4 ¶27].

E0054.summary: Collective witness that knowledge of the Magistery comes rather by Inspiration of Heaven.
E0054.body: Cited in support that knowledge of the Magistery comes rather by Inspiration of Heaven: “This truth is acknowledged by all artists” [IV.3 ¶16].

E0055.summary: The philosophers just cited, whose combined evidence Atwood says yields the definition of the stone as purified Ethereality.
E0055.body: Atwood draws from their combined evidence the definition of the stone as purified Ethereality [I.2 ¶44].

E0056.summary: Part of a seven-letter riddle quoted from Hermes, followed by Yda and Liber; not explained.
E0056.body: Quoted from Hermes as part of the seven-letter riddle: “for Alpha follows, viz.: Yda and Liber” [I.3 ¶37]. The text gives no explanation here.

E0057.summary: Cited for calling the matter a stone.
E0057.body: Cited in support of calling the matter a stone: “Si lapis proprium nomen haberet lapis esset nomen ejus” [I.3 n13] (ours: 'If the stone had a proper name, stone would be its name').

E0058.summary: First of the alchemists' three periods of the threefold Law: the objective Light, the ether above.
E0058.body: Atwood names Altitude, with Latitude and Profundity, as the Alchemists' three periods of the threefold Law, and states: “the Altitude is the objective Light, the ether that is above” [III.3 ¶72]. Asserted identity: Altitude = the objective Light, the ether that is above [III.3 ¶72].

E0059.summary: Ambrose and Phillip Muller, German writers listed among persecuted adepts.
E0059.body: Listed among persecuted adepts and among the German writers, with works cited as *Philippi Mulleri Miracula et Mysteria Medico-Chemica* and Amb. Muller's *Paradeis-Spiegel* [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70, I.1 n78].

E0060.summary: Teacher who, Atwood relates, admitted an ass daily to his lectures alongside Origen and Porphyry.
E0060.body: Cited as illustration: he admitted an ass daily to his lectures, alongside Origen and Porphyry [III.2 ¶64].

E0061.summary: In a quoted Platonic Successor, the impulse toward the First, which the passions impede.
E0061.body: Quoted from the Platonic Successor: “the passions alone, which impede our anagogic impulse to the First” [II.4 ¶41]. The text gives no further gloss.

E0062.summary: Augustine's third mode of vision, as Atwood reports it: drawn above, beholding intelligible species by pure infusion of light into the understanding.
E0062.body: Atwood reports Augustine's third mode of vision: “the third is anagogic, and an intellectual sight, drawn above, by which intelligible species are beheld” [II.4 ¶15]. It is a pure infusion of light into the understanding and occurs in Elysium. Asserted identity: anagogic = intellectual sight [II.4 ¶15].

E0063.summary: Called by Atwood one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School; cited for Intellect as separating principle, the ignited Stone as inner Sun, and as an alchemist.
E0063.body:
Atwood calls him 'one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School' and cites his lost works as preserved by Simplicius (via Taylor's note to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*) for Intellect's efficient, separating operation: “Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing” [III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶22, III.1 n27]. What he describes as past, internal philosophers describe as present; his “it begins from that which is small to exercise its comprehending power” she applies to starting with a small portion [III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶32]. He “calls it Intellect”, naming the One Thing in consciousness [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶35]; matter is the progeny of mind [III.2 ¶40].

His 'ignited Stone' Atwood identifies with the inner Sun, saying he was discredited through the error that he meant the visible sun [II.3 ¶54]; he identifies the central earth with the Salt of Saturn (“hands loftily”) [II.3 ¶41].

Celebrated as an alchemist, author of the *boke of Conversions Naturall*, praised by Norton as the plainest writer; his metaphysics agrees with Aristotle's [I.1 ¶14, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16]. Within the Ordinal he is cited for “Nemo prima fronte reperitur discretus” [IV.1 ¶26].
